Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot air balloon drifting over rows of lavender at sunset, with a lone tree on a golden hill

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

12 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The balloon, upper left (frame 20% to 36% across, 3% to 33% down), with the sun on the horizon as a second bright point Light: The setting sun, low on the horizon a little left of center (frame 43% across, 41% down). Highlights face it: the left side of the tree crown, the top rim of the golden hill, the tops of the lavender rows, the lower right of the balloon.How this lesson was made

Tubes

  • Titanium white

  • Orange

  • Ultramarine

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: covering and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 flat: cloud circles and streaksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: the sun diskRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #10 flat: the ridges and slopesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat: tapping the leaf clustersOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #4 flat: filling the stripesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • Liner (#1 or #0): ropes and basketLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #4 round: the brightest tips and path lightRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

STEP 1 OF 12

Paint the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the sun, low on the horizon a little left of center (37% across, 41% down).
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Evening blue, X-stroke a band across the top 8% of the canvas.
  3. X-stroke Peach glow from 8% to 30% down, blending into the blue while both are wet.
  4. X-stroke Sun gold from 30% to 45% down, brightest at the sun's spot. Below it, X-stroke Cloud coral down to a straight, level edge at 62% (6.8 inches from the top).
  5. Smooth the joins with long side-to-side strokes. Leave the canvas below 62% white. Let the sky dry.
Paints for this step4 paints, 4 new
  • Evening blue new2 parts milky white, 1 part dark ultramarine, a touch of light magenta
  • Peach glow new2 parts flesh tint, 1 part orange, a touch of light magenta
  • Sun gold new1 part yellow deep, a touch of flesh tint, a touch of milky white
  • Cloud coral new1 part orange, 1 part permanent red, 1 part milky white

Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first.

Mix plenty of Sun gold: it covers the biggest area.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

X stroke. Criss-cross the flat in overlapping X shapes so neighboring colors blend with no hard line.

Long horizontal blend. Finish with light side-to-side strokes the full width to calm the X marks.

Watch out: Don't stop the sky at the mountains. Running it to 62% keeps the strokes long, and the mountains and fields go over it.

Watch out: Stop blending as soon as the paint drags; streaks can stay.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 12

Paint the clouds and the sun

  1. Let the sky dry. With the #8 flat and creamy Cloud rose, circle in the cloud bases where the picture shows them.
  2. That's a big mass across the right half (from 46% across, top to 30% down, sloping to 42% at the right edge) and a bank on the left (to 16% across, 5% to 35% down).
  3. Circle Cloud coral over each cloud's middle, and dab coral streaks between 25% and 38% down. In the blue at the top, circle a few thumbnail-size coral cloudlets.
  4. Touch Cloud gold on the cloud edges facing the sun, mostly their lower edges.
  5. With the #6 round and Sun cream, paint the sun: a disk 0.7 inch wide at 37% across, 41% down. Dab Sun gold around it.
Build the depth, dark first

Brushes

#8 flat#6 round

Strokes

Small circles. Swirl the flat's corner in small overlapping circles to give each cloud a bumpy, soft edge.

Dabbing. Tap short strokes of coral for the broken streaks; don't drag them smooth.

Watch out: Each value covers less than the one before. Leave the rose showing.

Watch out: Sun cream over gold may need a second coat once dry.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 12

Paint the far mountains

  1. Let the clouds dry. With the #10 flat and creamy Mountain violet, paint the ridges in horizontal strokes.
  2. The range is highest at the left edge (37% down), dips to a valley under the sun, peaks at 59% across, 40% down, dips at 72%, and rises to 40% at the right edge.
  3. Fill down to a level edge at 56% down. The gold sky still shows from 56% to 62%.
  4. Brush Mountain shadow on the slopes facing away from the sun, and Mountain lilac on the slopes facing it.

Horizontal strokes. Keep the flat level and pull long strokes; slant only along the ridge lines.

Watch out: Keep the far mountains soft and flat, with no texture.

Watch out: Don't cover the sun: its lower edge just touches the valley.

STEP 4 OF 12

Paint the far fields

  1. Let the mountains dry. With the corner of the #10 flat and Far green, dab a band of far trees from 46% to 53% down, from the left edge to 75% across.
  2. Tap a little Field gold on the tops of the bumps, leaving the dark below.
  3. Brush Field gold below in horizontal strokes, from 52% to 58% down.
  4. Dab a bumpy row of Far green from 56% down to the straight edge at 62%. The right quarter stays mountains and sky; the hill covers it next.

STEP 5 OF 12

Paint the golden hill

  1. Let the fields dry. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Field gold, paint the hill's top edge.
  2. It runs from 28% across at 61% down, up through 58% across at 53% down and 75% at 48%, to the right edge at 44% down.
  3. Fill below that line to 62% down, with curved strokes that follow the slope.
  4. With the corner of the #10 flat, dab short slanted Hill olive strokes in patches across the lower and right part, then Hill light flecks on top, more near the rim. Leave gold between them.
  5. Tap a bumpy Far green row along the hill's bottom edge, to the right edge.

STEP 6 OF 12

Paint the lone tree

  1. Let the hill dry. With the #6 round and Wood brown, pull the trunk up thick-to-thin from 86% across, 46% down, to 40% down, about 0.3 inch wide, forking as in the diagram.
  2. With the old stiff flat, tap Tree dark green into a wide rounded crown from 74% across to the right edge, 20% to 42% down.
  3. Tap Tree mid green clusters through the middle, then Tree light green on the left clusters facing the sun.

#6 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Thick-to-thin. Press the round at the trunk base and ease off as you pull up into each branch, so it tapers.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff flat with little paint; each tap leaves a clump of leaves.

Watch out: Leave dark green showing between clusters, or the crown goes flat.

Watch out: Try a few taps on scrap paper first.

STEP 7 OF 12

Block in the lavender rows and paths

  1. Let the hill dry. Dot the vanishing point at 56% across, 61% down.
  2. With the #10 flat and Path sienna, pull two straight paths from the dot: the left one 26% to 36% across at the bottom edge, the right one 75% to 86%, as in the diagram.
  3. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Lavender violet, fill the rest from 61% down to the bottom, each stroke pulled along its row toward the dot.
  4. With the #10 flat, draw Lavender shadow lines between rows, about six on each side, wide in front and thin near the dot.

Brushes

#10 flat1 inch flat

Strokes

Strokes toward a vanishing point. Start each stroke at the front and pull it toward the dot, so the rows narrow and bunch together at the back.

Watch out: Keep the paths straight: check them with the brush handle held from the dot.

Watch out: The painting looks rough at this stage. That's normal; the texture comes next.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 12

Paint the balloon's stripes

  1. Let the sky dry. With the #6 round and thin paint, outline the balloon as in the diagram: a circle about 2.7 inches wide, 10% to 29% across, tapering to a point at 20% across, 27% down.
  2. With the #4 flat and creamy paint, fill nine stripes left to right: Balloon red, Balloon blue, Balloon red, Balloon orange, Balloon blue, Balloon red, Balloon yellow, Balloon blue, Balloon orange.
  3. Curve each stripe with the balloon: the middle stripe straight, the outer ones bowing out at the widest part, all meeting at the point.

STEP 10 OF 12

Dab the lavender's dark marks and stems

  1. Let the field dry. With the 1 inch flat and Lavender shadow, brush the whole field darker in strokes pulled toward the dot. Leave the paths. Let it dry.
  2. With the #10 flat, streak Wood brown along each path toward the dot.
  3. With the #6 round and Stem green, flick short stems upward along the front rows, the bottom 15% of the canvas, longest at the very bottom.
  4. With the old stiff flat and creamy Lavender violet, dab along every row: big dabs in front, tiny near the dot. Leave dark between dabs.

Brushes

#6 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Strokes toward a vanishing point. Pull the dark wash along each row toward the dot, as in step 7.

Flicking. Light load, quick upward flick from the row base, so each stem tapers.

Dabbing. Tap short upright dabs along each row; overlap them in front, space them out at the back.

Watch out: Cover the whole field in one pass, not one area at a time.

Watch out: Test a few flicks on scrap first.

Add the brightest highlights

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A hot air balloon over lavender rows at sunset, with a lone tree on a hill

Found in the image: just the picture (a painting, no screenshot parts)

Done: none

Why: Nothing around the picture to cut.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: the left 11% (cloud and lavender) and the right 4% (sky and hill edge)

Why: The photo is 3:2 and the canvas 14:11; trimming the sides keeps the balloon, sun, and tree whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, a village of houses, cypresses, and scattered bushes. Hundreds of items: yes, every lavender stalk. Detail inside big shapes: yes, veined clouds. More than 8 parts: yes.

Changed: Dropped the village, cypresses, and bushes; merged the distant fields into gold and olive bands and the clouds into a few soft masses; turned the lavender into rows of loose dabs, darker at the base; kept the balloon's stripes, the sun, the tree, and the straight paths.

Why: An 11x14 at beginner level holds about 8 big parts and one-mark textures.

A sunset paint-along: a striped balloon in a coral sky over converging lavender rows. The pull is the color (orange sky against a purple field); the hard parts are the dense lavender texture and keeping the rows and paths converging on one point. The lesson teaches the vanishing-point layout and builds the lavender in passes.

Subject: A striped hot air balloon drifting over rows of lavender at sunset, with a lone tree on a golden hill
Focal point: The balloon, upper left (frame 20% to 36% across, 3% to 33% down), with the sun on the horizon as a second bright point
Light: The setting sun, low on the horizon a little left of center (frame 43% across, 41% down). Highlights face it: the left side of the tree crown, the top rim of the golden hill, the tops of the lavender rows, the lower right of the balloon.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sunset sky gradient
  2. clouds and the sun
  3. far mountains
  4. far fields and tree band
  5. golden hill
  6. lone tree
  7. lavender rows and the two paths
  8. balloon stripes
  9. balloon shading, neck, ropes, and basket
  10. lavender dark marks and stems
  11. lavender light tips
  12. brightest highlights
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named it (acrylic-paint-along-beginner).

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Back-to-front paint-along suits a landscape with a sky, distance, and a textured foreground, and it's how the owner paints.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

The owner named the paint-along technique; block-in adds a sketch and block-in stage the owner's YouTube-style practice skips.

How the paint recipes were worked out31 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order12 steps

Sky first, run past the horizon; then clouds and sun, mountains, far fields, the hill, the tree, the lavender block-in; then the balloon (the subject) over the finished sky; then the lavender texture in passes; the brightest touches last.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky

    Covers the top 62% so the mountains and fields go over it without white gaps.

  2. 2. Paint the clouds and the sun

    Clouds sit on the dry sky; the sun is the brightest point and goes on with them.

  3. 3. Paint the far mountains

    Farthest land, soft and flat.

  4. 4. Paint the far fields

    The next distance band; only the left 75%, since the hill covers the rest.

  5. 5. Paint the golden hill

    Nearer than the fields, painted over them.

  6. 6. Paint the lone tree

    Sits on the hill, so after it.

  7. 7. Block in the lavender rows and paths

    Lays out the perspective flat before any texture, so the dab passes have rows to follow.

  8. 8. Paint the balloon's stripes

    The subject, over the finished sky; flat stripes first.

  9. 9. Shade the balloon and add the basket

    The teacher's second layer: shading, then neck, ropes, and basket.

  10. 10. Dab the lavender's dark marks and stems

    First texture pass over the whole field: dark wash, stems, violet dabs.

  11. 11. Add the light lavender tips

    Second pass: lighter tips on top.

  12. 12. Add the brightest highlights

    Brightest touches last.

Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Three shaped or laid-out things got diagrams (the tree, the lavender field's perspective, the balloon); the rest are fills, bands, or one repeated mark.

  • Step 6: Paint the lone tree beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object appears whole, and where the branches fork from the trunk isn't clear in the picture.

    Pieces: A Y trunk, then one wide dark crown of overlapping circles, then mid and light clusters on the sun side, the way a teacher builds a leafy tree.

  • Step 7: Block in the lavender rows and paths beginner check

    Noticed: The rows and paths depend on one vanishing point; describing every row's angle would take a paragraph.

    Pieces: A dot at 56% across, two straight paths from it, then rows pulled toward it, drawn as a 100 x 31 band at the field's real shape.

  • Step 8: Paint the balloon's stripes beginner check

    Noticed: The subject's shape (a circle tapering to a point) and its curved stripes.

    Pieces: A big circle for the top, a tapered bottom to a point, then stripes that bow out and meet at the point.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A gradient; the bands are named in order with their heights.
  • Step 2: Clouds are one repeated mark (small circles) with a values table; the sun is a disk with a size and position. The text reviewer proposed a one-puff diagram; the values table and stroke already carry it.
  • Step 3: A ridge line given by its peaks and dips; soft and flat.
  • Step 4: Three level bands with heights.
  • Step 5: One slope given by four points along its top edge, plus dabbed texture. The reviewer's patch diagram would repeat the dabbing stroke.
  • Step 9: Shading on named stripes and a small basket with a position; the step image shows it.
  • Step 10: One repeated mark over rows already laid out.
  • Step 11: One repeated mark on the row tops.
  • Step 12: A few touches; the picture shows where.

It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • canvas-view takes file names inside the lesson folder; given a full path it silently wrote canvas/output/<lesson>/99_finish.png. It could strip the lesson prefix or refuse.
  • The mixer's swatch snap can land on a dark gap instead of the thing named (Stem green snapped to near-black between rows). Thin things like stems need a hand-checked sample spot.
  • lock-steps fixed a render that stopped the sky short (clouds-sun) for free, because the gap was outside the step's region. Worth trying before a redo when the problem is outside the step's boxes.
  • My first plan put the right path at 65-78% across at the bottom; it's 75-83%. Measuring path edges by pixel color, not by eye on the grid, caught it.
  • The technique's beginner_version prompt doesn't name a palette, though the skill says it does; I added the owner's paints to it by hand.
  • The text review found the lavender dab step's picture also darkens the whole field. A 'wash the field darker' pass belongs in the plan between the flat rows and the dabs; the research notes cover dark-then-light passes but not a toned wash under a dense texture.
  • The text reviewer had no PIL in its Python, so it couldn't zoom into the balloon to check the stripe order.
  • With the 30-tube owner palette, the mixer reaches for whatever tubes fit best per paint, so the 31 paints use 28 tubes and What you need lists nearly everything (Milky white, Cashew, Flesh tint, black, gray among them). The mixer could prefer tubes already used in the lesson, or cap the tube count, so the shopping list stays short.
